question: The EU Deforestation Regulation1 (EUDR) imposes extensive requirements for traceability, geolocation and legality documentation. However, agricultural and feed sector actors continue to face uncertainty regarding practical implementation. Differing interpretations could create unnecessary administrative burdens and disrupt supplies to the EU feed and livestock sectors. 1.

What scientific, technical and economic evidence supports requiring physical segregation of EUDR-compliant bulk soy rather than allowing a verifiable administrative chain-of-custody model based on mass balance, documentation and an audit trail, ensuring that EUDR-compliant soy placed on the EU market does not exceed the documented quantity entering the system?

How will the Commission ensure that credible national traceability and certification systems can be used for companies’ due diligence, allowing existing controls and data to be reused and avoiding duplication, and can audit reports from such schemes be accepted as ‘adequately conclusive and verifiable information’ without requiring companies to reproduce evidence already audited by accredited independent third parties?

How will the Commission ensure uniform interpretation of legality documentation across Member States based on a risk-based approach, and what legal status does it attribute to FAQs and guidance where they go beyond or further specify the requirements of the EUDR?

Regulation (EU) 2023/1115 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 31 May 2023 on the making available on the Union market and the export from the Union of certain commodities and products associated with deforestation and forest degradation and repealing Regulation (EU) No 995/2010 (OJ L 150, 9.6.2023, p. 206, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2023/1115/oj). 1
